actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Grid-Based Latent 3D Representations for Appearance Capture
PROPOSAL: Compare 3D object reconstruction quality and efficiency of various popular grid-based latent representations (e.g., NerfNet, Voxelize, Occupancy Networks, etc.) on a suite of challenging real-world datasets (e.g., Kitti, DIODE, etc.) with control over the grid resolution, spatial complexity, and density.
CONTROLS: Standard grid-based methods (e.g., Chen et al., 2018; Mescheder et al., 2019) and state-of-the-art appearance models (e.g., Naseer et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020).
COST: 300 GPU-hours (assuming ~1 billion parameter models, 30k samples per run, 10 datasets, and batch sizes of 32)
PREDICTION: We expect that high-resolution grid-based models will achieve good 3D reconstruction results for simple and moderate geometric complexity objects and that performance will degrade for highly complex or reflective objects. Performance may even fail for objects with very rough or detailed surfaces.

(To systematically understand popular approaches' limitations before implementing novel, specialized representations for appearance.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structure-Aware SDF Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel view-dependent 3D representation that combines signed distance fields (SDFs) with a learned, sparse structure-aware grid to better capture objects' complex geometry and appearance in real-world settings. The model will generate object reconstructions by progressively computing SDFs for points while selectively refining the sparse grid in areas of interest, allowing for adaptive, coarse-to-fine representation learning. We expect this approach to improve the resolution and geometric detail of the reconstructed models while accounting for view-dependent appearance variations.
CONTROLS: Standard grid-based methods (e.g., Chen et al., 2018; Mescheder et al., 2019), standard appearance models (e.g., Naseer et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020), and a baseline that simply adds appearance embeddings to grid-based models in a simple Euclidean space.
COST: 900 GPU-hours (accounting for large batch sizes, multiple stages of refinement, and varying complexity in datasets)
PREDICTION: We expect SDF-transient-invariance with some tricks to provide orders of magnitude more detail than traditional occupational state, while potentially breaking when materials get too lossy for local connections or a sparse grid starts reaching acceptable losses at natural surfaces via thinner local error curves resisting periodically (# CC clustering failures).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Structure-Aware SDF Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel view-dependent 3D representation that combines signed distance fields (SDFs) with a learned, sparse structure-aware grid to better capture objects' complex geometry and appearance in real-world settings. The model will generate object reconstructions by progressively computing SDFs for points while selectively refining the sparse grid in areas of interest, allowing for adaptive, coarse-to-fine representation learning. We expect this approach to improve the resolution and geometric detail of the reconstructed models while accounting for view-dependent appearance variations. An additional key feature of the model is to directly condition on image data, by using a proxy model to generate an informative image mask for SDF refinement, thus enabling single-image 3D reconstruction and object synthesis.
CONTROLS: Standard SDF-based models (e.g., Park et al., 2020; Ivan et al., 2020) and appearance models that attempt single-image 3D reconstruction (e.g., Yariv et al., 2020; Sitzmann et al., 2019)
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (accounting for multiple runs with varied spatial and appearance complexities)
PREDICTION: We expect the new model to achieve significantly better results compared to traditional SDF-based models on real-world 3D object reconstruction and single-image 3D image-based rendering tasks, with potentially reduced limitations from view-dependent appearance capture, a good performance score near baseline or surpassed by energy-rich established, suggesting this feature of structure detail held actually behave link lack further bump tone.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: View-Dependent Appearance Modeling using Neural Texture Fields
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel neural texture field (NTF) model that captures view-dependent appearance variations of 3D objects by encoding spatially-varying texture maps onto the object surface. The NTF will be represented as a 3D grid of texture maps, each parameterized by a neural network that predicts texture attributes (color, normal, specular, etc.) based on the object's 3D geometry, local coordinate systems, and image features. This approach will enable the generation of photorealistic renderings of objects with complex, view-dependent appearances under various lighting conditions.
CONTROLS: Standard texture-based appearance models (e.g., Smith et al., 2020; Paschalidou et al., 2020) and recent progress in neural texture modeling (e.g., Zhang et al., 2020; Schawndt et al., 2018)
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (accounting for complex texture grid refinement and multiple texture map simulations)
PREDICTION: We expect the NTF model to provide state-of-the-art performance in view-dependent appearance modeling and rendering, capable of capturing subtle variations in texture attributes that are difficult for existing models to reproduce.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Learning of 3D Object Representations with Primed Ray Marching
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel framework that combines unsupervised learning of 3D object representations with ray marching-based rendering. The framework will be trained to generate high-quality 3D renderings of objects from random viewpoints, enabling the discovery of new latents that capture both geometric and view-dependent appearance properties. Our proposed approach will utilize a combination of adversarial and KL-divergence-based regularization terms to encourage the generated latents to capture accurate object geometry and realistic appearance properties.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art unsupervised 3D object representation learning methods (e.g., van der Smagt et al., 2019; Reizenstein et al., 2020)
COST: 2400 GPU-hours (accounting for multiple ray marching iterations and diverse 3D object rendering scenarios)
PREDICTION: We expect the framework to learn compact and expressive 3D object representations that generalize across various object categories, lighting conditions, and viewpoints, with the potential to produce top-notch results in a variety of 3D rendering and object generation tasks

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Rendering Resolutions on 3D Object Representations
PROPOSAL: Conduct an extensive investigation into the impact of rendering resolutions on the performance of state-of-the-art 3D object representation learning models. Our study will include experiments with varying rendering resolutions (e.g., low-resolution lut half to high-fidelity rendering), different rendering algorithms, and multiple metrics for evaluating the quality of generated 3D models. We will analyze how different rendering resolutions affect the latent representations learned by the models, and identify any potential limitations or biases introduced by varying rendering resolutions.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art 3D object representation learning methods (e.g., Mescheder et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020) and various rendering resolution settings
COST: 600 GPU-hours (accounting for numerous rendering iterations and multiple model evaluations)
PREDICTION: We expect the results to show that the quality of generated 3D models improves with increasing rendering resolutions, but also highlight some potential limitations of current 3D object representation learning methods that may be sensitive to changes in rendering resolution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Real-World Generalization of 3D Object Representations with Self-Supervised Pre-Training
PROPOSAL: Explore the efficacy of self-supervised pre-training for improving the real-world generalization of 3D object representations learned by state-of-the-art models. Our approach will involve pre-training a 3D object representation model on a large, synthetic dataset and then fine-tuning it on real-world data. We will compare the performance of self-supervised pre-training against other pre-training methods (e.g., supervised, adversarial) and analyze the impact of pre-training on real-world 3D object representation learning.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art 3D object representation learning methods (e.g., Sitzmann et al., 2019; Yariv et al., 2020) and various pre-training methods
COST: 900 GPU-hours (accounting for multiple pre-training and fine-tuning iterations)
PREDICTION: We expect the results to demonstrate the benefits of self-supervised pre-training for improving the real-world generalization of 3D object representations, and provide insights into the most effective pre-training strategies for this task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Effect of Dataset Distributions on 3D Object Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of dataset distributions on the quality of 3D object representations learned by state-of-the-art models. We will analyze the effect of different dataset characteristics (e.g., object complexity, pose diversity, lighting variations) on the learned representations and compare the performance of models trained on datasets with varying distributions. This study will help to identify the key factors that affect the generalizability of learned 3D object representations and provide insights into the choice of datasets for 3D representation learning.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art 3D object representation learning methods (e.g., Park et al., 2020; Ivan et al., 2020) and various dataset distributions
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (accounting for multiple dataset generation and model training iterations)
PREDICTION: We expect the results to highlight the importance of dataset quality and diversity for learning generalizable 3D object representations, and provide practical recommendations for dataset selection and generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Benchmark for Evaluating View-Dependent 3D Object Representations
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating view-dependent 3D object representations, consisting of a diverse set of real-world 3D object datasets, multiple evaluation metrics, and a standardized framework for comparing the performance of different 3D representation learning methods. This benchmark will enable a thorough comparison of state-of-the-art view-dependent 3D object representation models and provide insights into their strengths and limitations.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art view-dependent 3D object representation learning methods (e.g., Structure-Aware SDF Reconstruction, Neural Texture Fields) and various evaluation metrics
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (accounting for dataset preparation, model evaluations, and benchmark maintenance)
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed benchmark to become a valuable resource for the 3D computer vision community, facilitating the development and evaluation of view-dependent 3D object representation models and contributing to the advancement of this field.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: 3D Latent Representation with View-Dependent Appearance via Neural Radiance Fields
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether Neural Radiance Fields (NRFs) can learn a compact 3D latent representation that captures both geometry and view-dependent appearance by training on a dataset of real-world objects with multiple views.
CONTROLS: Compare NRFs with state-of-the-art geometry-only latent representations (e.g., Occupancy Networks, 3D Point Cloud Generative Adversarial Networks) on metrics such as geometric accuracy, view-dependent appearance fidelity, and model size/complexity.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: NRFs will improve geometric accuracy and view-dependent appearance fidelity compared to geometry-only representations, at the cost of increased model size and complexity. This approach will be limited by the availability of high-quality, multi-view datasets for training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Neural Radiance Fields for Single-Image 3D Object Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether conditioning Neural Radiance Fields (NRFs) on a single input image can improve their ability to generate a 3D object that matches the input viewpoint and appearance, by training on a dataset of real-world objects with paired images and 3D ground-truth.
CONTROLS: Compare conditioned NRFs with vanilla NRFs and state-of-the-art single-image 3D reconstruction methods (e.g., Sμεν́clic, Pix2Vox) on metrics such as geometric accuracy, view-dependent appearance fidelity, and reconstruction time.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Conditioned NRFs will improve geometric accuracy and view-dependent appearance fidelity compared to vanilla NRFs, and outperform state-of-the-art single-image reconstructions on both metrics. This approach will be limited by the availability of high-quality, paired image-3D data for training.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED 3: Conditional Neural Radiance Fields with Variational Autoencoder for Geometry-Appearance Disentanglement
PROPOSAL: Modify the Conditional Neural Radiance Fields (NRFs) from Proposal 2 to incorporate a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to disentangle geometry and appearance, enabling better transfer learning and view point-invariant feature learning, and investigate whether this combination can improve both single-image 3D reconstruction and generalization across new views.
CONTROLS: Compare VAE-conditioned NRFs with vanilla NRFs and state-of-the-art geometry-appearance disentanglement methods (e.g., Primitive-based VAEs, Structured VAEs) on metrics such as geometric accuracy, view-dependent appearance fidelity, and transfer learning performance.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (due to the added complexity of VAE training)
PREDICTION: VAE-conditioned NRFs will improve both single-image 3D reconstruction and generalization across new views, by enabling effective geometry-appearance disentanglement and transfer learning. This approach will require careful VAE design and training to avoid over-simplification of the learned factors.

ACTION: REVISE 2

PROPOSAL: Modify the Conditional Neural Radiance Fields (NRFs) to learn a coarse->fine refinement pipeline, where the coarse stage predicts the object's bounding box and orientation, and the fine stage refines the prediction by conditioning on a higher-resolution input image.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Baseline 3D Point Distribution Field Models
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate two popular baseline 3D point distribution field (PRAFT) models: Patch-based PRAFT and Pointcloud PRAFT, on the real-world ScanNet dataset, focusing on density-based evaluation metrics such as mean and standard deviation of mesh area. Assess the limitations of these models in representing view-dependent appearance and fine-grained details in geometry.
CONTROLS: Compare results to the standard ScanNet evaluation protocol, and evaluate the PRAFT models without class-specific appearances to isolate the effect of appearance on the representation.
COST: 500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: These models will struggle to capture view-dependent appearance and fine-grained details, showing limitations in representing an object's full appearance. High variations in mesh area suggest difficulties in execution. This baseline study will provide a foundation for our novel approach.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Fusing Dense Voxel Grids with Multimodal Appearance Information
PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of a novel 3D representation that integrates a dense voxel grid with a multimodal appearance encoder, which produces a separate output for each reflection sphere around an object. Train and evaluate this representation on the BlendedMVS dataset, which contains real-world RGB and volumetric representations of objects, using metrics such as multi-scale angular IoU and SSD.
CONTROLS: Compare results to the standard BlendedMVS evaluation protocol and the voxel-grid alone, and evaluate the multimodal appearance encoder with various input configurations (e.g., different numbers of reflection spheres) to analyze its impact on performance.
COST: 750 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This representation will show improvements in geometry and appearance reconstruction compared to PRAFT models, but may suffer from overfitting due to the high-dimensional voxel grid and multimodal appearance encoder outputs. We expect moderate gains on metrics like multi-scale angular IoU.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Baseline 3D Point Distribution Field Models
PROPOSAL: Expand the baseline study to include three additional PRAFT models, in addition to Patch-based and Pointcloud PRAFT: Conditional PRAFT, Message-Passing PRAFT, and Signed Distance Signed Distance Function PRAFT. Assess the strengths and limitations of these variants using the same evaluation metrics as before on the ScanNet dataset.
CONTROLS: Maintain comparison to the standard ScanNet evaluation protocol and evaluate these models without class-specific appearances to isolate the effect of appearance on the representation.
COST: 1250 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This expanded evaluation will reveal the relative performance of the different PRAFT models, highlighting the role of conditional factors and message-passing in geometry-only representations. The Signed Distance Signed Distance Function PRAFT may show more accurate reconstruction results for complex scenes but at higher complexity costs.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Fusing Dense Voxel Grids with Multimodal Appearance Information
PROPOSAL: Introduce the following refinements to the novel 3D representation that integrates a dense voxel grid with a multimodal appearance encoder: replace the separate output for each reflection sphere with a learnable, view-dependent feature attachment for each octree level, and modify the appearance encoder to learn separately for diffuse, specular, and ambient lighting, enabling more accurate representation of view-dependent effects. Trains and evaluate this enhanced model on the BlendedMVS dataset using updated metrics such as Learned-Focal-Angle-Suppressed metric and Reflections-aware-3D-mIoU.
CONTROLS: Compare results to the updated standard BlendedMVS evaluation protocol, and evaluate the multimodal appearance encoder using workflows varying in how appearance source types (e.g., diffuse, specular) are encoded to show interests in how representation modeling the appearance field could diversify.
COST: 1100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This enhanced model will show improved performance in view-dependent geometry and appearance reconstruction by addressing limitations of prior attempt and resultantly demonstrates concrete benefit over baseline voxel grid and multimodal appearance model.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Generating Realistic 3D Objects from Single RGB Images
PROPOSAL: Integrate a novel diffeomorphic registration module into the 2D image-to-3D transform network to improve the alignment of generated 3D objects with the input image. This module will enable better estimation of the camera-to-world transformation and subsequent viewpoint-consistency under various lighting conditions. ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Scalability and Generalization of View-Dependent 3D Representations
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scalability and generalization of the proposed view-dependent 3D representations by training and evaluating them on a large-scale real-world dataset, such as the Project HOAX benchmark, that contains a diverse set of 3D objects with varying geometries, appearances, and illumination conditions. Assess the performance of the representations on tasks such as viewpoint-agnostic 3D reconstruction, viewpoint-consistency assessment, and generalization to unseen viewpoints and lighting conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare results to state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction methods and evaluate the generalization capacity of the representations by testing them on Never Seen Before (NSB) Real objects from Industrial Settings.

PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate the scalability and generalization capabilities of the proposed view-dependent 3D representations, enabling their application to a wide range of real-world tasks and scenarios, and highlighting their potential to improve the efficiency and realism of 3D object generation and reconstruction in various industries.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Single-Step AR Generator via Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We design a meta-learning framework where the one-step generator is learned as part of a metagorithm, which predicts the optimal generator parameters based on the teacher AR model's conditional token distributions. The framework is meta-trained across a set of synthetic AR tasks with varying token lengths and densities. At test time, the meta-learned algorithm selects the best generator parameters for the teacher AR model and fine-tunes the one-step generator in a single step.
CONTROLS: Compare with single-step generator trained without meta-learning, distill/decompose the teacher AR model, replace the AR model with a VAE/GAN model and train a one-step generator on it. 
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This meta-learning approach may partially mitigate the training speed issue of DD1, but its performance drop relative to the teacher AR model might remain substantial due to the representation mismatch.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distillation of Local Conditional Distributions
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel distillation method that fine-tunes the one-step generator by directly learning local conditional distributions of token distributions, instead of learning the global token distribution like DD1. This method encourages the one-step generator to capture the complex relationships between the encoded tokens, potentially improving the model's representation learning capacity.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original DD1 method, apply the proposed distillation method to other generator architectures, replace the distillation loss with the KL-divergence between local and global distributions.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method might improve the one-step generator's quality by capturing more information from the teacher AR model, but may lead to overfitting or map ill-conditioning for certain inputs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  REVISED - Single-Step AR Generator via Hierarchical Representations
PROPOSAL: We modify the single-step AR generator via meta-learning to use a hierarchical representation of the token sequence, where each layer in the hierarchy captures a higher-level abstraction of the token relationships. The one-step generator is then trained to predict the token distributions at each layer, allowing it to capture both local and global token dependencies.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original meta-learning approach, use different types of hierarchical representations (e.g., convolutional, recurrent, or attention-based), reduce the number of layers in the hierarchy.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised method may improve the one-step generator's quality and robustness by capturing a wider range of token dependencies, but may require more explicit engineering of the hierarchical representation and may not be efficient for very long sequences.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:  REVISED - Single-Step AR Generator via Meta-Learning with Attention
PROPOSAL: We modify the single-step AR generator via meta-learning to incorporate an attention mechanism, which selectively focuses on the most relevant tokens in the sequence when predicting the next token distribution. The attention weights are learned as part of the meta-learning process, allowing the model to adaptively weight the importance of different tokens.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original meta-learning approach without attention, use different attention mechanisms (e.g., self-attention, interraction-based attention), evaluate the impact of attention on model performance.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised method may enhance the one-step generator's ability to capture long-range dependencies and adapt to varying input sequences, potentially leading to improved performance and robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Generate from Noisy Teacher Estimates
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach that learns to generate from noisy teacher estimates, which are obtained by adding Gaussian noise to the token distributions predicted by the teacher AR model. The one-step generator is then trained to reconstruct the noise-corrected distributions, allowing it to learn robust and flexible token relationships even when the teacher's estimates are imperfect.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original teacher AR model, add different types of noise (e.g., uniform, Laplacian), evaluate the impact of noise level on generator performance.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may improve the one-step generator's generalization and robustness by learning to correct for noise in the teacher's estimates, but may require careful tuning of the noise level and amount of training data.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED - Distillation of Local Conditional Distributions with Adaptive Decoding
PROPOSAL: We modify the distillation of local conditional distributions to use an adaptive decoding mechanism that adjusts its decoding resolution based on the complexity of the local token space. The decoding resolution is dynamically updated during training, allowing the one-step generator to efficiently capture complex local relationships and adapt to varying input sequences.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original distillation method without adaptive decoding, evaluate the impact of decoding resolution on generator performance, use different adaptive decoding mechanisms (e.g., dynamic decoding, hierarchical encoding).
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised method may improve the one-step generator's ability to capture complex local relationships and adapt to varying input sequences, potentially leading to improved performance and robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Training for One-Step Generators
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised training method for one-step generators that utilizes the teacher AR model's predictions as pseudo-labels for the target sequence. The one-step generator is trained to reconstruct the pseudo-labels, allowing it to learn robust and flexible token relationships without relying on explicit ground-truth labels.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original teacher AR model, use different pseudo-labeling mechanisms (e.g., self-labeling, multi-labeling), evaluate the impact of pseudo-label quality on generator performance.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method may improve the one-step generator's generalization and robustness by learning from pseudo-labels, but may require careful tuning of the pseudo-labeling mechanism and may not be effective for very low-quality pseudo-labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for One-Step Generators
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning framework for one-step generators that trains the model to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, such as image synthesis and text-to-image translation. The model learns to adapt to different input spaces and modalities, potentially leading to improved robustness and generalization.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original one-step generator, use different task combinations (e.g., image generation, segmentation, and captioning), evaluate the impact of task number and difficulty on generator performance.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method may improve the one-step generator's robustness and generalization by learning to adapt to different tasks and modalities, but may require careful task selection and weighting to avoid VANISHING GRADIENTS during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Post-Hoc Evaluation of One-Step Generators
PROPOSAL: We propose a post-hoc evaluation framework for one-step generators that assesses the model's ability to capture semantic and syntactic relationships in the target sequence. The framework uses a combination of metrics, such as semantic similarity and syntax trees, to evaluate the model's performance on tasks such as image captioning and text-to-image translation.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original one-step generator, use different evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE, SPICE), evaluate the impact of evaluation metric on generator performance.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the one-step generator's strengths and weaknesses, but may require careful selection of evaluation metrics and may not be effective for very complex tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED - Learning to Generate from Noisy Teacher Estimates with Multi-Step Refining
PROPOSAL: We modify the learning to generate from noisy teacher estimates method to include a multi-step refining process that iteratively refines the estimates based on the generated tokens. This process allows the model to learn more robust and accurate token relationships, potentially leading to improved performance on tasks such as image captioning and text-to-image translation.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original learning to generate from noisy teacher estimates method, use different multi-step refining mechanisms (e.g., recursive refinement, feedback loop), evaluate the impact of refining steps on generator performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised method may improve the one-step generator's ability to learn robust and accurate token relationships, but may require careful tuning of the refining mechanism and may not be effective for very noisy teacher estimates.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Autoregressive Model Properties and Sampling Inefficiencies
PROPOSAL: Investigate the theoretical properties of autoregressive image models, specifically their sequential modeling and conditioning dependencies, and analyze their implications on sampling efficiency. Formulate and prove a worst-case bound on the number of sampling steps required for a given level of accuracy, demonstrating the fundamental tradeoff between step count and sample quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art image synthesis models, and assess the generalizability of these results to other sequential modeling tasks.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation will provide a rigorous understanding of the challenges inherent in autoregressive image modeling and highlight the need for efficient, one-step sampling methods. The derived bound may indicate that achieving single-step sampling without performance degradation is theoretically infeasible for some aspects of AR models.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating DD1’s Noise-to-Data Mapping
PROPOSAL: Examine the determinism-preserving flow matching process in DD1's noise-to-data mapping using various codebook sizes and datasets. Analyze the distribution of the constructed mapping and assess its learnability by the subsequent distilled model. Investigate how larger codebooks impact the mapping's complexity, the model's training, and the overall performance in the one-step sampling setting.
CONTROLS: Compare DD1's performance to the original AR model, assess the impact of the noise-to-data mapping, and evaluate the effect of different codebook sizes (e.g., 256, 1024, 4096) on the model's performance and training speed.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may reveal insights into the challenges of learning the noise-to-data mapping in DD1, providing a better understanding of the performance degradation associated with one-step sampling in this approach. By analyzing the distribution of the mapping and its impact on the model, we can identify potential improvements and potential limitations of the current method.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Single-Step Sampling via enjoying Predictive Information
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of predictive information, such as self-supervised reconstruction losses or auxiliary objectives (e.g., adversarial losses), to improve the efficiency and quality of autoregressive sampling. Investigate whether incorporating these objectives into the model's training process enables the model to learn a more informative, conditionally-independent representation of the image, facilitating one-step sampling without significant performance degradation.
CONTROLS: Compare the effect of different predictive information objectives, assess the trade-off between sampling efficiency and model performance, and evaluate the robustness of this approach to varied codebook sizes and datasets.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may uncover new opportunities for improving the efficiency and quality of autoregressive image synthesis by leveraging predictive information. By incorporating these objectives, the proposed approach could enable single-step sampling while maintaining, or even improving, the model's generation capabilities compared to existing one-step methods.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE:  Single-Step Sampling via Utilizing Conditional Informativeness
PROPOSAL: Extend the proposal 3: Explore the use of predictive information, such as self-supervised reconstruction losses or auxiliary objectives (e.g., adversarial losses), to improve the efficiency and quality of autoregressive sampling. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Bound on One-Step Generator Training
PROPOSAL: We prove that training a one-step generator to match the output distribution of a well-trained teacher AR model is NP-hard, assuming the generator is a neural network with ReLU activations, the teacher AR model provides a probability of the next token conditioned on all previous tokens, and we want the generator to take a latent variable as input.
CONTROLS: A reduction from the clique problem in Boolean satisfiability.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical work).
PREDICTION: We expect to establish a lower bound on the sample complexity of one-step generator training, which may explain why existing methods struggle to achieve high-quality generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Baseline One-Step Generator using Flow Matching
PROPOSAL: We implement a one-step generator that uses flow matching in the codebook embedding space to directly generate a complete token sequence from a noise token, without relying on a predefined noise-to-data mapping or any additional models. The generator is trained to match the output distribution of a well-trained teacher AR model, using a binary cross-entropy loss between the predicted and target token distributions.
CONTROLS: We compare our baseline against a control group where we train the same one-step generator using a variant of the DD1 model that defines a fixed, predefined noise-to-data mapping.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (training a baseline model on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect our baseline to perform worse than the original AR model, but better than methods that have failed to achieve single-step sampling without significant performance degradation, and it should provide a useful lower bound on the quality of one-step generators.

ACTION: REVISE
PROPOSAL: A Baseline One-Step Generator using Flow Matching
REVISED PROPOSAL: We implement a one-step generator that uses flow matching in the codebook embedding space to directly generate a complete token sequence from a noise token, without relying on a predefined noise-to-data mapping or any additional models. We compare three variants of our baseline: (1) Directly training the generator with the teacher AR model as a probability oracle, (2) using an auxiliary decoder to approximate the probabilities for the generator, and (3) jointly training an encoder-decoder architecture that outputs the token probabilities directly.
CONTROLS: We compare our baseline against the DD1 model, the teacher AR model, and ablations of our model where we either remove the flow matching component or the auxiliary decoder.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (training a baseline model on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect variant (2) to perform best among the ablations, as the auxiliary decoder helps to approximate the output distribution of the teacher AR model.

We compare three variants of our baseline: (1) Directly training the generator with the teacher AR model as a probability oracle, (2) using an auxiliary decoder to approximate the probabilities for the generator, and (3) jointly training an encoder-decoder architecture that outputs the token probabilities directly.
CONTROLS: We compare our baseline against the DD1 model, the teacher AR model, and ablations of our model where we either remove the flow matching component or the auxiliary decoder.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (training a baseline model on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect variant (2) to perform best among the ablations, as the auxiliary decoder helps to approximate the output distribution of the teacher AR model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Examining the Role of Temperature in One-Step Generator Training
PROPOSAL: We explore the impact of temperature scaling on the performance of one-step generators, and investigate whether warmup or cool-down techniques during training can improve convergence and stability. We experiment with different temperature schedules for the teacher AR model and the generator, and analyze the effects on generation quality and diversity.
CONTROLS: We compare our findings against the results of directly training the generator with the teacher AR model as a probability oracle (variant (1) of our baseline), and against a control group where we train the generator without temperature scaling.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect that temperature scaling can improve the performance of one-step generators, particularly when used in conjunction with warmup or cool-down techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for One-Step Generators
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of adversarial training to improve the performance of one-step generators. We add a discriminator to our system, and train the generator and discriminator in an adversarial fashion, where the generator tries to produce tokens that are indistinguishable from real tokens in the dataset, and the discriminator tries to differentiate between real and generated tokens.
CONTROLS: We compare our adversarial trained generator against the results of directly training the generator with the teacher AR model as a probability oracle (variant (1) of our baseline), and against a control group where we train the generator without adversarial training.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect that adversarial training can improve the performance of one-step generators, particularly in terms of image quality and diversity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical One-Step Generator for Large-Scale Images
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical one-step generator architecture that consists of multiple stages, each stage generating a coarser-scale token sequence than the previous one. This allows us to generate high-resolution images in a single forward pass, by hierarchically refining the token sequence from coarse to fine scales.
CONTROLS: We compare our hierarchical generator against the results of directly training the generator with the teacher AR model as a probability oracle (variant (1) of our baseline), and against a control group where we train the generator without hierarchical refinement.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect that our hierarchical generator can efficiently generate high-resolution images in a single forward pass, with improved image quality and diversity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Minimum Description Length (MDL) Objective for One-Step Generator Training
PROPOSAL: We propose a new training objective for one-step generators based on the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. The MDL objective combines the generation quality and the complexity of the generator, allowing us to automatically adjust the trade-off between these two aspects.
CONTROLS: We compare our MDL-based objective against the results of directly training the generator with the teacher AR model as a probability oracle (variant (1) of our baseline), and against a control group where we train the generator without the MDL objective.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect that the MDL objective can improve the performance of one-step generators, by promoting more efficient and effective utilization of the generator's capacity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Performance of One-Step Generators on Real-World Image Generation Tasks
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the performance of the one-step generators proposed in this set on various real-world image generation tasks, including image-to-image translation, image inpainting, and image super-resolution. We compare the performance of our generators against state-of-the-art methods on these tasks, and analyze the strengths and weaknesses of each generator.
CONTROLS: We use a set of public benchmarks and evaluation metrics to compare the performance of our generators against the state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a real-world dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect that our one-step generators will show competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods on these real-world image generation tasks, and provide insights into the advantages and limitations of one-step generator architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open-Source One-Step Generator Implementation
PROPOSAL: We release an open-source implementation of our one-step generator architectures, along with a comprehensive set of pre-trained models and examples, to facilitate further research and development in this area.
CONTROLS: We make our code available on GitHub, and provide documentation and tutorials to help users get started with the implementation.
COST: negligible, as the cost is mostly about code maintenance and documentation.
PREDICTION: We expect that our open-source implementation will facilitate collaboration and innovation in the field of one-step generator research, and lead to the development of new and improved generator architectures.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structure-Based Cross-Entropy Training for MoE Models
PROPOSAL: We will train MoE models with a modified cross-entropy loss that incorporates a structure-based term. Specifically, we will use an auxiliary classifier that estimates the correct expert for each input token, using the normalized weight of the selected experts as features. The classification loss is added to the standard cross-entropy loss, and we use a weight decay term on the shared weights of the classifier. This structure-based training encourages experts to specialize and discourages homogenization by providing a more explicit signal for routing diversity.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed method against two baselines: (1) standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training, and (2) standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training with the load-balancing term.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed method to achieve better expert specialization and more efficient routing, resulting in improved performance on downstream tasks, particularly language modeling and mathematical reasoning. The proposed method may fail to generalize well to tasks that require more holistic overviews, such as reading comprehension.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Meta-Routing for Dynamic Expert Learning
PROPOSAL: To encourage experts to adapt to changing input distributions and specialize further, we will implement an online meta-routing mechanism that adjusts the weights of the router adaptively during training. Specifically, we will use an online meta-learning algorithm to learn a set of meta-routes that are conditioned on the current input batch. These meta-routes are obtained by taking the top-k experts that have the highest load-balancing values for the current batch, and the online meta-learning algorithm learns to adjust the weights of the router to match the meta-routes.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed online meta-routing against two baseline methods: (1) full-batch routing, where the router is updated only once every full batch, and (2) standard meta-routing with a fixed set of meta-routes.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed online meta-routing to improve performance on tasks that require adaptability to changing input distributions, such as language modeling and exam-style knowledge question answering. However, it may be computationally expensive and may not generalize well to tasks with complex input sequences, such as reading comprehension.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Structure-Based Cross-Entropy Training for MoE Models
REVISED PROPOSAL: To further improve the structure-based training method, we will add a regularizer that encourages the shared weights of the auxiliary classifier to be orthogonal to the shared weights of the MoE model. This orthogonal regularizer will help to reduce the correlation between the classifier and the MoE model, and ensure that the classifier is learning meaningful features about the expert weights.
CONTROLS: We will compare the revised structure-based training method against the previous version, as well as against the standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training with the load-balancing term.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised structure-based training method to achieve even better expert specialization and more efficient routing, resulting in improved performance on downstream tasks. The orthogonal regularizer may have a small impact on the overall performance, but it is expected to be beneficial.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cluster-Based Routing for Expert Heterogeneity
PROPOSAL: To promote expert heterogeneity and prevent expert homogenization, we will cluster the input tokens into groups based on their similarity, and then use a separate router for each cluster. Each router is responsible for selecting experts that are specialized in a specific aspect of the input data. We will evaluate the clusters using a clustering quality metric, such as silhouette score, and select the clusters that are most representative of the input data.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed cluster-based routing against the standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training with the load-balancing term.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed cluster-based routing to encourage expert heterogeneity and promote more diverse expert specializations, resulting in improved performance on downstream tasks. However, it may be computationally expensive and may not generalize well to tasks with noisy or missing input data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Modulating Experts for Adaptive Routing
PROPOSAL: To improve expert routing and adaptability, we will propose a self-modulating expert mechanism that allows experts to adjust their own routing weights based on their performance and relevance to the input data. Each expert will maintain a self-modulation score that indicates its confidence in its own routing weight. The scores will be updated online based on a reward signal that encourages experts to route to relevant and task-specific tokens.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed self-modulating experts against the proposed online meta-routing method.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed self-modulating experts to improve the adaptability and routing efficiency of experts, resulting in improved performance on downstream tasks. However, it may lead to expert instability and inconsistent routing behaviors if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Specific MoE Routing for Downstream Tasks
PROPOSAL: To promote expert specialization for downstream tasks, we will propose task-specific MoE routing that adapts the routing weights of experts based on the specific downstream task. We will store a set of task-specific routing weights that are learned for each downstream task, and use a task-conditional routing mechanism to select the routing weights based on the task type.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed task-specific MoE routing against the proposed structure-based cross-entropy training and the standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training with the load-balancing term.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed task-specific MoE routing to improve the performance of MoE models on downstream tasks by promoting expert specialization and adaptability to specific task requirements. However, it may lead to increased computational cost and training complexity due to the need to store and adapt task-specific routing weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exposing Expert Knowledge with Attention and Token Reduction
PROPOSAL: To provide more insights into expert knowledge and routing decisions, we will use attention mechanisms to highlight the most relevant tokens selected by each expert and reduce the dimensionality of the input data by sampling a subset of tokens. We will analyze the attention weights and token distributions to reveal expert-specific knowledge and identify potential cases of expert homogenization.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed expert knowledge analysis against the standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training with the load-balancing term, and examine the expert attention weights and token distributions as a diagnostic tool.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed expert knowledge analysis to provide valuable insights into expert learning and reveal new opportunities for expert guidance and improvement. However, it may require additional computational resources and time for attention weight computation and analysis.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Cluster-Based Routing for Expert Heterogeneity
REVISED PROPOSAL: To further improve the cluster-based routing method, we will add a dynamic clustering mechanism that adaptively updates the clustering assignments based on the input tokens' representations learned by the MoE model. We will use a clustering quality metric, such as silhouette score, to evaluate the clustering assignments and update the clustering assignments at regular intervals during training.
CONTROLS: We will compare the revised cluster-based routing against the original cluster-based routing and the proposed online meta-routing method.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised cluster-based routing to adapt more effectively to changing input data distributions and promote more stable and efficient expert specialization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: MoE Training with Importance-Sampled Routing
PROPOSAL: To reduce the variance and improve the stability of MoE training, we will propose a training method that uses importance-sampling-based routing. We will first estimate the importance of each expert's routing weights using a secondary estimation algorithm, and then weight the each expert's contribution to the overall loss using these importance estimates. This can help to stabilize the training process and improve the quality of expert learning.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed importance-sampled routing training against the standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training with the load-balancing term.
COST: 12 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed importance-sampled routing training to improve the stability and efficiency of MoE training, but may require careful tuning of the importance estimation algorithm.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Evaluation and Comparison of MoE Routing Methods
PROPOSAL: To evaluate and compare the performance of the proposed MoE routing methods on a large scale, we will conduct a systematic evaluation of all proposed methods on four downstream tasks: English language modeling, Chinese language modeling, mathematical reasoning, and exam-style knowledge question answering. We will use a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics, including perplexity, accuracy, and F1-score, to compare the performance of each routing method.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the proposed MoE routing methods against the standard teacher-forcing cross-entropy training with the load-balancing term.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the large-scale evaluation to provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each MoE routing method and enable us to identify the most effective methods for different downstream tasks. However, the large-scale evaluation may require significant computational resources and time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structured Routing Regularization for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: Train MoE models with structured routing regularization, where a new loss term encourages experts to specialize in specific subspaces of the input data, such as text prefix length or part-of-speech tags. This regularization will be achieved by matching the expert activation patterns with pre-defined templates, and the quality of pattern matching will be measured by a self-supervised objective function that auto-generates labels for training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Explicitly Guided Expert Routing for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel training objective for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which we call "Focused-Expert-Routing" (FER). FER introduces a term to the standard MoE loss function that encourages experts to develop specialized representations by maximizing the similarity of their outputs with the model's output on a given prompt. This can be achieved by including a term in the loss function that measures the cosine similarity between the output of the model and a given expert's output, maximizing over the output of the model for each prompt. We expect this term to guide the routing process and induce expert specialization.
CONTROLS: We will compare FER with both the standard MoE loss function and the standard MoE loss function augmented with a load-balancing regularization that encourages uniform expert usage. We will evaluate both variants on the next 7 experiments.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (approximate)
PREDICTION: FER is expected to improve expert specialization and, consequently, the overall performance of the MoE model on downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning and exam-style knowledge question answering. The improved expert specialization can lead to better generalization and lower degrees of expert homogenization. However, the introduction of FER might lead to performance degradation on tasks where the MoE model has to deal with diverse inputs or environments that require a combination of different skills, in which case writing code can be too radical.

TITLE: Investigating the Micro- and Macro-Effects of Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the effects of expert specialization on the MoE's performance at both the micro- and macro-level. At the micro-level, we will analyze the intra-expert representation quality, expert-ensemble coherence, and learnability within and across experts. At the macro-level, we will examine how expert specialization affects the MoE's ability to handle task heterogeneity, adaptation to new tasks, and optimization of the routing mechanism. We expect that expert specialization will lead to improved representation quality, ensemble coherence, and adaptability, but potentially reduce learnability due to redundancy or over-specialization. To address these aspects, we will employ a battery of carefully designed experiments and tasks.

This approach aims to leverage the strengths of individual experts while promoting collaboration and adaptability. We will train MoE models with this hierarchical softmax routing mechanism and evaluate their performance on a range of tasks, including mathematical reasoning and exam-style knowledge question answering. We expect this approach to improve the MoE's ability to handle task heterogeneity and adapt to new tasks.

TITLE: Meta-Learning for MoE Model Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a meta-learning approach to adapt the Mixture-of-Experts model to new tasks with minimal training data. The meta-learning framework will be trained to learn a good initialization of the MoE model for a wide range of tasks, with the goal of achieving fast adaptation to new tasks. We will use a variety of meta-learning algorithms, including Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) and Reptile, to adapt the MoE model to new tasks. We expect this approach to improve the MoE model's ability to generalize to new tasks and adapt to changing environments.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of the meta-learned MoE model on a range of tasks and compare it to the standard MoE model trained from scratch.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the meta-learned MoE model will achieve faster adaptation to new tasks and improve overall generalization performance, especially in situations where expertise thresholds are met optimally.

TITLE: Evaluating the MoE Model on Downstream Tasks with Varying Expertise Requirements
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the MoE model on a range of downstream tasks with varying expertise requirements, including mathematical reasoning, exam-style knowledge question answering, and reading comprehension. We will analyze how the MoE model's performance changes as the expertise requirements of the tasks differ, and how the different routing mechanisms (standard, FER, ER, hierarchical softmax) affect its performance. We expect to see that the MoE model will perform best on tasks that align with its learned expertise, and worst on tasks that require novel combinations of expertise.
CONTROLS: We will run experiments on a set of tasks with varying expertise requirements and compare the performance of the MoE model with different routing mechanisms.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the MoE model will demonstrate expertise-dependent performance, with better performance on tasks that require its learned expertise and worse performance on tasks that require novel combinations of expertise.

We propose a novel training objective for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which we call "Focused-Expert-Routing" (FER). FER introduces a term to the standard MoE loss function that encourages experts to develop specialized representations by maximizing the similarity of their outputs with the model's output on a given prompt. This can be achieved by including a term in the loss function that measures the cosine similarity between the output of the model and a given expert's output, maximizing over the output of the model for each prompt. We expect this term to guide the routing process and induce expert specialization.

PROPOSAL 4: Investigating the Micro- and Macro-Effects of Expert Specialization
We propose to investigate the effects of expert specialization on the MoE's performance at both the micro- and macro-level. At the micro-level, we will analyze the intra-expert representation quality, expert-ensemble coherence, and learnability within and across experts. At the macro-level, we will examine how expert specialization affects the MoE's ability to handle task heterogeneity, adaptation to new tasks, and optimization of the routing mechanism. We expect that expert specialization will lead to improved representation quality, ensemble coherence, and adaptability, but potentially reduce learnability due to redundancy or over-specialization. PROPOSAL 5: Expert Ensembling via Hierarchical Softmax Routing
We propose to develop a novel routing mechanism that utilizes hierarchical softmax to ensemble experts at different levels of abstraction. This approach aims to leverage the strengths of individual experts while promoting collaboration and adaptability. We will train MoE models with this hierarchical softmax routing mechanism and evaluate their performance on a range of tasks, including mathematical reasoning and exam-style knowledge question answering. We expect this approach to improve the MoE's ability to handle task heterogeneity and adapt to new tasks.
Controls: We will compare the performance of MoE models with hierarchical softmax routing to those using standard MoE loss function, FER, and ER, each with and without self-isolation regularization.
Estimated cost: 900 GPU-hours (estimated)
Prediction: We anticipate that hierarchical softmax routing will lead to better performance on tasks requiring adaptability and generalization, as it allows for more efficient collaboration between experts at different levels of abstraction.

PROPOSAL 6: Meta-Learning for MoE Model Adaptation
We propose to develop a meta-learning approach to adapt the Mixture-of-Experts model to new tasks with minimal training data. The meta-learning framework will be trained to learn a good initialization of the MoE model for a wide range of tasks, with the goal of achieving fast adaptation to new tasks. We will use a variety of meta-learning algorithms, including Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) and Reptile, to adapt the MoE model to new tasks. We expect this approach to improve the MoE model's ability to generalize to new tasks and adapt to changing environments.
Controls: We will evaluate the performance of the meta-learned MoE model on a range of tasks and compare it to the standard MoE model trained from scratch.
Estimated cost: 800 GPU-hours (estimated)
Prediction: We anticipate that the meta-learned MoE model will achieve faster adaptation to new tasks and improve overall generalization performance, especially in situations where expertise thresholds are met optimally.

PROPOSAL 7: Evaluating the MoE Model on Downstream Tasks with Varying Expertise Requirements
We propose to evaluate the MoE model on a range of downstream tasks with varying expertise requirements, including mathematical reasoning, exam-style knowledge question answering, and reading comprehension. We expect to see that the MoE model will perform best on tasks that align with its learned expertise, and worst on tasks that require novel combinations of expertise.

Estimated cost: 1000 GPU-hours (estimated)
Prediction: We anticipate that the MoE model will demonstrate expertise-dependent performance, with better performance on tasks that require its learned expertise and worse performance on tasks that require novel combinations of expertise.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Dynamic Multi-Label Image Classification with Joint Component Adaptation

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of a meta-learner to adaptively adjust the configuration of a multi-label image classifier's core components during training, taking into account the interactions between augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function. This will involve using a reinforcement learning (RL) framework to learn a policy that selects the best component configurations at each training stage, based on a reward function that encourages good performance on the validation set.

CONTROLS: Compare to a static configuration baseline, with ablations of the meta-learner and RL framework to analyze their individual contributions. Use two real-world benchmarks: Pascal VOC and OpenImages V7.

COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The adaptive meta-learner will outperform the static configuration baseline, especially on the rare labels and in terms of training stability and convergence speed. However, the approach may struggle with optimization efficiency due to the increased complexity of the training process.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Multi-Component Attention for Joint Optimization

PROPOSAL: Develop a novel attention mechanism that integrates attention weights for each of the four core components (augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function), allowing the model to dynamically weight their contributions during training. This will enable the model to adaptively focus on the most relevant components at each stage of training, potentially improving optimization efficiency and accuracy.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline and proposal 1, with ablations of the attention mechanism and its individual components to analyze their contributions. Use the same two real-world benchmarks as before.

COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The multi-component attention mechanism will provide a significant boost to the model's performance, particularly in terms of optimization efficiency and rare label handling. However, it may suffer from instability due to the added complexity of the attention weights.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Transferable Task Conditioners for Adaptive Learning-Rate Scheduling

PROPOSAL: Introduce a transferable task conditioner that learns to adjust the learning rate for each training stage, taking into account the evolving characteristics of the task and the current state of the model. This conditioner will be trained in a meta-learning framework, enabling it to transfer knowledge across tasks and stages, and making it adaptable to different multi-label image classification problems.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline, proposal 1, and proposal 2, with ablations of the transferable conditioner and its components to analyze their contributions. Use the same two real-world benchmarks as before.

COST: Estimated 30 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The transferable task conditioner will improve the model's performance by providing adaptable and informed learning-rate adjustments, particularly in scenarios with changing task characteristics. However, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning and regularization to prevent overfitting to specific tasks or stages.

ACTION: REVISE

TITLE: REVISE: Transferable Task Conditioners for Adaptive Learning-Rate Scheduling

PROPOSAL: Revise proposal 3 to incorporate a more principled approach to learning the learning-rate schedule, based on the expected information gain of the current training stage. This will involve using a variant of the Bayesian optimization algorithm that takes into account the uncertainty of the learning rate and the potential benefits of exploration. The goal is to develop a more adaptive and efficient learning-rate scheduling mechanism that balances exploration and exploitation.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline, proposal 1, and proposal 2, with ablations of the Bayesian optimization approach and its components to analyze their contributions. Use the same two real-world benchmarks as before.

COST: Estimated 35 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The revised transferable task conditioner will provide more robust and adaptive learning-rate scheduling, leading to improved performance and efficiency. However, it may require careful tuning of the Bayesian optimization hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: REVISE 3

TITLE: Transferable Task Conditioners for Adaptive Loss Functions

PROPOSAL: Revise proposal 3 to focus on the adaptive selection of loss functions for multi-label image classification. The transferable task conditioner will learn to adjust the weighting of different loss components (e.g. cross-entropy, focal loss, triplet loss) based on the evolving characteristics of the task and the current state of the model. This will enable the model to dynamically shift attention towards the most informative loss components and improve the overall performance.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline, proposal 1, and proposal 2, with ablations of the transferable conditioner and different loss functions to analyze their contributions. Use the same two real-world benchmarks as before.

COST: Estimated 35 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The revised transferable task conditioner will provide improved performance by adaptively selecting the most informative loss components for the task at hand. However, it may require careful tuning of the weighting scheme to avoid overfitting to specific tasks or stages.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Ablation Study on Inter-Component Coordination

PROPOSAL: Conduct an extensive ablation study to analyze the effects of inter-component coordination on the performance of the multi-label image classifier. This will involve systematically removing or modifying the interactions between different components (e.g. disabling the attention mechanism between the optimizer and loss function, or removing the transferable task conditioner from the learning-rate scheduling module) and assessing the impact on the model's performance.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline, proposal 1, proposal 2, and proposal 3, with a focus on understanding how different inter-component coordination mechanisms contribute to the overall performance.

COST: Estimated 60 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The ablation study will provide valuable insights into the importance of inter-component coordination for multi-label image classification, and inform the design of more effective adaptation mechanisms. However, it may require significant computational resources and careful experimental design to avoid confounding variables.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Inter-Component Conflict Detection and Resolution

PROPOSAL: Develop a mechanism to detect and resolve conflicts between different components of the multi-label image classifier. This will involve using a conflict detection module to identify situations where the optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function are working against each other, and a resolution mechanism to adaptively adjust the component configurations to mitigate these conflicts.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline, proposal 1, proposal 2, proposal 3, and the ablation study, with a focus on evaluating the effectiveness of conflict detection and resolution in improving overall performance.

COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The conflict detection and resolution mechanism will provide significant improvements in performance, particularly in scenarios with complex inter-component interactions. However, it may require careful tuning of the conflict detection thresholds and resolution strategies to avoid over-adaptation or under-adaptation.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Online Ensemble Approach for Multi-Label Image Classification

PROPOSAL: Develop an online ensemble approach that combines the strengths of different component configurations to improve the overall performance of the multi-label image classifier. This will involve maintaining an ensemble of models, each trained with a different component configuration, and adaptively switching between them based on the current training stage and performance.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline, proposal 1, proposal 2, proposal 3, proposal 4, and proposal 5, with a focus on evaluating the effectiveness of the online ensemble approach in improving overall performance.

COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The online ensemble approach will provide significant improvements in performance, particularly in scenarios with rapidly changing training data or task requirements. However, it may require careful tuning of the ensemble members and switch strategy to avoid over-adaptation or under-adaptation.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Emphasis on Rare Label Handling for Real-World Applications

PROPOSAL: Modify the existing component adaptation approaches to prioritize rare label handling, a critical requirement for real-world multi-label image classification tasks. This will involve integrating a rare label emphasis module into the existing adaptation mechanisms, such as the transferable task conditioner or the online ensemble approach, to ensure that the model accurately identifies and handles rare labels.

CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline, proposal 1, proposal 2, proposal 3, proposal 4, proposal 5, and proposal 6, with a focus on evaluating the effectiveness of rare label handling in real-world scenarios.

COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The emphasis on rare label handling will significantly improve the model's performance on real-world tasks, particularly those with a large class imbalance. However, it may require careful tuning of the rare label emphasis module to avoid over-adaptation to rare labels at the expense of more common labels.

ACTION: REVISE 7

TITLE: Emphasis on Rare Label Handling for Real-World Applications

PROPOSAL: Revise the rare label emphasis module to incorporate a self-supervised learning component that encourages the model to explore and understand the underlying class relationships and dependencies between rare and common labels. This will involve injecting artificial rare label noise into the training data and using it to guide the model's adaptation.

CONTROLS: Compare to the revised baseline, proposal 1, proposal 2, proposal 3, proposal 4, proposal 5, proposal 6, and the original emphasis on rare label handling, with a focus on evaluating the effectiveness of the self-supervised rare label exploration in real-world scenarios.

COST: Estimated 140 GPU-hours.

PREDICTION: The revised rare label emphasis module will provide even better performance on real-world tasks with rare labels, particularly those with a large class imbalance. The self-supervised learning component will enable the model to automatically identify and explore the complex relationships between labels, leading to more accurate and robust handling of rare labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a computationally efficient, joint model-configuration adaptation method called ACL: Adaptive Configuration Learning. ACL dynamically updates the four core training components during training: augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function. ACL utilizes meta-learning to adapt the configuration based on the model's evolving state and training dynamics. For each training step, ACL Retrieves relevant historical configurations from a learned memory, modifies them to suit the current training stage, and Applies the updated configuration to fine-tune the model. ACL includes a data-providing module to effectively measure the model's utility and a performance-enhancing module to efficiently learn from past experience. The model is trained with a re-weighting loss to ensure no under-exploitation, over-exploitation, or skipping the proposal steps happening simultaneously.
CONTROLS: We compare ACL against six state-of-the-art, static-configuration pipelines, including AutoAugment, SMOTE, and AdamW- scheduler coupled methods. We also show the ablation study for different sub-modules and configurations of ACL.
COST: Approximately 250 GPU-hours for a full experiment
PREDICTION: Compared to static configuration pipelines, ACL will significantly outperform on benchmark validation metrics, yielding higher accuracy (especially for rare labels) and F1 score of 6-8%.
