ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Hierarchical Learning-Rate Scheduling for ACL
PROPOSAL: While ACL's ability to dynamically adjust multiple training components is a significant improvement, we recognize that the choice of learning-rate schedule remains a crucial factor in its success. In this proposal, we introduce an Efficient Hierarchical Learning-Rate Scheduling (EHRLS) method, specifically tailored for ACL. EHRLS is a hierarchical multi-resolution technique that initially adjusts the learning rate for the global task and then hierarchically refines it for the individually learned labels. EHRLS leverages incremental learning to dynamically adapt the learning rate during training, ensuring that all task-relevant labels receive appropriate exploration-exploitation trade-offs.
CONTROLS: Compare EHRLS against standard and state-of-the-art learning-rate schedules (e.g., cyclical, cosine, and AdamW) on ACL, both with and without FIC evaluation.
COST: Approximately 150 GPU-hours for fine-tuning
PREDICTION: By efficiently adjusting the learning rate, EHRLS will consistently increase ACL's overall validation accuracy on benchmark datasets by 3-5% compared to both standard and state-of-the-art learning-rate schedules.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Understanding Interaction Costs in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: To further explore the inter-component coordination and interaction costs, we revise the FIC framework to include a newly added 'label-aware' module. This module enables the framework to sensitivity analyze interaction costs on specific label subsets. This revised framework examines how the synergy between optimizer-augmentation combinations changes during the learning process on both global and local levels, providing more detailed insight into the model's performance for specific labels. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of the model under drifted conditions to identify how interaction costs adapt to changes in the data distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare label-aware FIC with the original FIC framework to determine the significant differences in their outputs.
COST: Approximately 120 GPU-hours for the synthetic dataset simulation
PREDICTION: The label-aware FIC will uncover notable, previously unknown interaction cost behavior and patterns in certain label subsets, yielding improvements in the overall model accuracy for rare labels by up to 2% on benchmark datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Based Configuration Adaptation for ACL
PROPOSAL: To further enhance ACL's adaptability, we introduce an Uncertainty-Based Configuration Adaptation (UBCA) module, which utilizes model uncertainty estimates to guide the configuration updates. UBCA computes the epistemic uncertainty of ACL's predictions for the current mini-batch and uses it as a signal to modify the configuration, adjusting augmentation, optimizer, learning rate, and loss function to address the underlying issues. This module enables ACL to adapt to changing data distributions and modeling uncertainties, reducing overconfidence and improving overall performance.
CONTROLS: Evaluate UBCA in combination with ACL and EHRLS, both separately and jointly. Compare to state-of-the-art models that also utilize uncertainty-based methods.
COST: Approximately 180 GPU-hours for evaluation and comparison
PREDICTION: The incorporation of UBCA into ACL will improve performance on benchmark datasets by up to 12% for rare labels, particularly under drifting conditions, and enhance the overall stability and robustness of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Data Transferability and Generalization Analysis for ACL
PROPOSAL: While ACL and its variants have demonstrated impressive performance on benchmark datasets, we aim to investigate its transferability and generalization capabilities on real-world data. We conduct a comprehensive study, collecting and processing multiple real-world datasets with varying characteristics, and evaluate ACL's performance on these datasets. Our analysis focuses on understanding how ACL adapts to diverse data distributions, model complexities, and task requirements.
CONTROLS: Compare ACL's performance across different real-world datasets, examining the impact of task relevance, data quality, and model complexity. Evaluate ACL against state-of-the-art models that also pursue data transferability.
COST: Approximately 300 GPU-hours for dataset collection, processing, and evaluation
PREDICTION: Our study will reveal ACL's real-world transferability and generalization capabilities, highlighting its strengths and weaknesses in adapting to diverse data distributions and model complexities. This analysis will inform future research directions and potential modifications to ACL to enhance its real-world applicability.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Understanding Interaction Costs in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We extend the label-aware FIC framework to include an optional neural network-based "critic" component that learns to value the interactions between different components. This critic network, trained in auxiliary mode, evaluates the quality of interactions and guides the adaptation process by incorporating its estimates into the FIC framework. This modification allows the FIC framework to learn dynamic interaction values, further enhancing its ability to understand the intricate relationships between components.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised FIC framework with and without the critic component to evaluate its impact on interaction cost analysis and model adaptation.
COST: Approximately 150 GPU-hours for training and evaluation
PREDICTION: The inclusion of the critic component will improve the FIC framework's ability to identify complex interaction patterns, leading to a 5-7% increase in model accuracy for rare labels on benchmark datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable and Decentralized ACL Architecture for Multi-Node Training
PROPOSAL: To scale up ACL for more complex and large-scale multi-label image classification tasks, we propose a scalable and decentralized ACL architecture that leverages multiple nodes for training. This architecture employes a novel optimization algorithm that coordinates the adaptations of the ACL components across nodes, while maintaining a shared memory space for configuration updates. This decentralized approach enables efficient training on large datasets, reduces the communication overhead, and accelerates the adaptation process.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the decentralized ACL architecture on large-scale benchmarks, comparing it to the original ACL and other state-of-the-art methods.
COST: Approximately 400 GPU-hours for large-scale training and evaluation
PREDICTION: The proposed decentralized ACL architecture will achieve a significant speedup in training time, up to 3-5 times faster than the original ACL, while maintaining comparable accuracy performance on large-scale benchmarks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) for ACL: Interactive Configuration Tuning
PROPOSAL: To provide an additional layer of control and fine-tuning for ACL, we propose a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) framework that allows users to interactively adjust the configuration updates. This framework leverages recent advances in human-computer interaction, graphical user interfaces, and AI-driven user experience design to enable users to intuitively explore the configuration space, inspect key decisions made by ACL, and fine-tune specific components or entire configurations. HITL is designed to reduce the expertise barrier for ACL adoption and improve its overall performance in challenging scenarios.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the usability and effectiveness of the HITL framework in conjunction with ACL, comparing it to other adaptive and static configuration approaches.
COST: Approximately 100 GPU-hours for prototyping and testing the HITL framework
PREDICTION: The HITL framework will provide significant improvements in ACL's usability and ease of use, reducing the expertise barrier by up to 40% for non-experts, while also leading to a 2-5% increase in model accuracy in challenging scenarios where human oversight and fine-tuning are most valuable.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We finalize and refine the ACL algorithm by incorporating the key insights and component improvements from the previous proposals. This revised ACL algorithm, dubbed "Advanced ACL," integrates a meta-learning framework for configuration adaptation, multi-resolution hierarchical learning-rate scheduling, uncertainty-based configuration adaptation, and a scalable decentralized architecture for large-scale training. Advanced ACL also incorporates the Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) framework for interactive configuration tuning. This comprehensive algorithm provides an optimized adaptive configuration learning framework for multi-label image classification tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare Advanced ACL against state-of-the-art configurations and adaptation methods, evaluating its robustness, efficiency, and accuracy in diverse multi-label image classification scenarios.
COST: Approximately 600 GPU-hours for thorough evaluation and comparison
PREDICTION: Advanced ACL will exhibit significant improvements in accuracy (up to 15%), stability, and adaptability for multi-label image classification tasks, solidifying its position as a leading algorithm in this field.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Configuration Optimization for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Experiment with a novel adaptive learning procedure, where the configuration of the core training components is optimized jointly and iteratively over the course of training, using a meta-loss function that balances validation performance and exploration-exploitation trade-off. We adapt a Random Search (RS) algorithm to this dynamic optimization setting, where at each iteration, the current configuration is sampled and evaluated; the probabilities for the next step are then updated to favor configurations with better validation performance. Specifically, we will use a lightweight multi-label classifier (e.g., a variant of the class-balanced focal loss model [1]) and apply the dynamic RS across multiple real-world datasets (e.g., OpenImages, COCO-stuff, and NUS-WIDE).
CONTROLS: We will compare the dynamic RS approach against three static optimization baselines: (1) Grid Search (GS) in the configuration space; (2) Random Search (RS), where we fix a pre-defined number of iterations; and (3) Staged-scheduling, where training choices are updated at predefined milestones based on a fixed set of recipes.
COST: 500 GPU-hours across multiple datasets.
PREDICTION: We expect the dynamic RS approach to outperform the static optimization baselines in terms of final performance and better handling of rare labels, but may struggle with overfitting to the meta-loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration of Component Interactions in Dynamic Configuration Optimization
PROPOSAL: Experiment with factorization-based ablation study to analyze the component interactions within the dynamic RS approach. Specifically, we will disentangle the effects of augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function on the overall training process and validation performance. For each interaction, we will design an orthogonal design matrix (e.g., a Hadamard matrix) to isolate the impact of one component while keeping others constant. This will enable us to better understand which interactions are most critical and where to focus our future optimization efforts.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the ablation study on the dynamic RS approach, and compare the results to the original approach.
COST: 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the ablation study to reveal that augmentation and loss function have the most significant impact on the dynamic RS approach, while optimizer and learning-rate schedule have relatively less effect, but still play important roles in fine-tuning the performance.

ACTION: ADD

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Calibration Set Size on Post-Training Quantization of 3D Reconstruction Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a series of experiments to study the effect of calibration set size on the performance of PTQ for VGGT, by quantizing its weights and activations using PTQ4ViT and testing the quantized models on a range of multi-view 3D reconstruction benchmarks, including camera pose estimation, point map, and point cloud reconstruction tasks, using the ModelNet40, the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository (S3DIS), and the 3D semantic scene understanding benchmark (3DSSG) datasets. Our controls will include a full-precision baseline and an uncalibrated PTQ counterpart to measure the impact of calibration on PTQ's performance.
CONTROLS: Full-precision VGGT, PTQ4ViT without calibration
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see diminishing returns in PTQ's performance as the calibration set size increases, with 100-200 samples being sufficient to achieve near-optimal performance. We also expect the effect of calibration set size to be more pronounced in camera pose estimation, which is a more challenging task than point map and point cloud reconstruction.

TITLE: Addressing the Heavy-Tailed Activation Statistics of Data-Independent Special Tokens in 3D Reconstruction Transformers
PROPOSAL: We propose to analyze and mitigate the impact of heavy-tailed activation statistics of data-independent special tokens on PTQ's performance. Specifically, we will study the effect of (i) applying a trimmed mean normalization, (ii) using max-min normalization, and (iii) clipping activations to a limited range, on the activation distribution of camera and register tokens in VGGT. We will then experiment with these normalization techniques in combination with PTQ4ViT and evaluate the effectiveness of each method on the same multi-view 3D reconstruction benchmarks and datasets used in our previous experiment.
CONTROLS: PTQ4ViT without normalization, PTQ4ViT with different normalization techniques
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that some form of normalization will effectively mitigate the impact of heavy-tailed activation statistics on PTQ's performance, while others may not be effective or could even degrade performance. Clipping may be a more aggressive technique that eliminates problematic activation statistics, but may also introduce issues with saturation or aliasing. The effectiveness of normalization techniques is likely to be task-dependent, with camera pose estimation benefiting more than point map and point cloud reconstruction tasks.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of knowledge distillation and pruning techniques to reduce the complexity of VGGT while maintaining its accuracy. Specifically, we will (i) distill the knowledge of VGGT into a smaller student model using a combination of forward knowledge distillation and reverse knowledge distillation, and (ii) prune the VGGT architecture using a combination of magnitude-based pruning and sparse pruning. We also expect that PTQ4ViT applied to the distilled and pruned models will result in comparable or improved performance compared to the original VGGT model.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate the robustness of PTQ4ViT to adversarial attacks on 3D reconstruction transformers, specifically VGGT. We will use a combination of black-box and white-box attacks to injecting perturbations into the input data and evaluate the performance of the PTQ4ViT model on the perturbed data. We will also compare the robustness of PTQ4ViT to the original VGGT model and analyze the impact of different calibration set sizes and normalization techniques on the robustness of PTQ4ViT.

We also expect that normalization techniques and calibration set size will have a significant impact on the robustness of PTQ4ViT, with larger calibration set sizes and suitable normalization techniques resulting in improved robustness.

This proposal addresses a critical aspect of PTQ4ViT, namely its robustness to adversarial attacks. We revise our previous proposal to also explore the use of a robust loss function, specifically the Huber loss, to mitigate the impact of heavy-tailed activation statistics on PTQ4ViT. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Methods Comparison for Simplifying the VGGT Transformer
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the effect of different model pruning techniques on the performance and memory requirements of VGGT. Specifically, we will apply state-of-the-art pruning methods such as ThiNet, FPGM, and LRT, and measure their impact on top-1 accuracy and FLOPs of the model. We will use the 'Four Seasons' dataset for evaluation, and train models with a fixed number of parameters in order to ensure that the variations in performance are due to the pruning techniques used.
CONTROLS: Baseline VGGT model, random pruning, weight sharing
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the pruning methods will have a limited impact on accuracy, with most of the decrease in FLOPs coming from more aggressive pruning, but with the corresponding accuracy dropoff. Hence, the choice of model pruning technique will be important for balancing performance vs. efficiency tradeoffs. However, it is less clear which techniques will generalize well to more complex multi-view 3D reconstruction datasets.

TITLE: Importance of Calibration Dataset Design for Post-Training Quantization
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the impact of calibration dataset selection and size on the quality of post-training quantization (PTQ) for VGGT. We will compare different strategies for generating calibration datasets, including randomly sampling from the training data, selecting edge cases, and generating synthetic data using GANs. We will measure the quality of PTQ using metrics such as calibration error and ROS misalignment across different calibration dataset sizes and types. The Controls will include a standard random sampling and no calibration setup. 
CONTROLS: Baseline PTQ, standard random sampling, no calibration, random sampling with edge cases sampling
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that carefully curated calibration datasets (selecting edge cases) will provide the best trade-off between calibration quality and computational cost. Additionally, using synthetic data with GANs will be particularly beneficial for generating diverse calibration datasets.

TITLE: Optimizing Quantization Strategies for Special Tokens
PROPOSAL: This experiment explores custom quantization strategies specifically designed for the special tokens in VGGT, such as camera and register tokens. We will investigate the impact of 1) channel-wise quantization, 2) split-quantization for the camera token, and 3) using quantization-aware learning (QAL) techniques for special tokens. We will compare the results using the 'ivasim' metric, which measures the reciprocal of the KL Divergence between the original and quantized distributions. This experimental design will allow us to examine the effectiveness of different quantization strategies for non-image data types and compare the results with the standard global expectation approach applied to all tokens in VGGT. 
CONTROLS: Standard global expectation quantization for special and image tokens, channel-wise quantization for all tokens, quantization-aware learning for all tokens, baseline model performance
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Since the special tokens are more complex and less representative of regular image data, we expect the results of channel-wise or split quantization to be notably different from the standard global expectation approach, but application of Quantization-aware learning techniques could bring performance back closer to baseline. However using quantization-aware learning  could also inflate the size of the calibration dataset.

TITLE: Analysis of Calibration Dataset Sampling Methods for VGGT Quantization
PROPOSAL: This experiment evaluates the impact of different sampling methods for generating calibration datasets for post-training quantization of VGGT. We will compare random sampling, stratified sampling, and cluster sampling, and investigate the effect of calibration dataset size on the model's 3D reconstruction performance. We will use metrics such as calibration error, bias-variance tradeoff, and 3D accuracy to evaluate the different sampling methods. Controls include a baseline calibration dataset generated using random sampling.
CONTROLS: Baseline random calibration, stratified calibration, cluster calibration
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that stratified or cluster sampling methods will lead to more accurate calibration datasets and better-performing VGGT models, especially as the size of the calibration dataset increases. However, we anticipate that the differences between these methods may be small, and that the choice of sampling method may depend on the specific characteristics of the 3D reconstruction dataset and the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Quantized VGGT to Out-of-Distribution Data
PROPOSAL: This experiment assesses the robustness of post-training quantized VGGT models to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We will evaluate the models on datasets with varying levels of authenticity and coherence, and examine their performance on tasks that require robustness, such as camera pose estimation and point map reconstruction. We will use metrics such as accuracy, FPS, and GPU memory usage to evaluate the robustness of the models. Controls include a baseline VGGT model and a baseline post-training quantized VGGT model trained on a clean dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline VGGT, baseline pre-quantized VGGT on clean data
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the post-training quantized VGGT models will exhibit a decrease in performance on OOD data compared to their in-distribution performance, but that the decrease will be more pronounced for certain datasets. We also anticipate that the choice of quantization strategy and calibration dataset size will impact the robustness of the models.

TITLE: Investigating Hardware-Aware Quantization for VGGT on Edge Devices
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the impact of hardware-aware quantization on the performance of VGGT on edge devices. We will explore different quantization techniques that are tailored to the constraints and characteristics of edge hardware, such as low-precision arithmetic units and energy-efficient processing. We will evaluate the performance of these techniques on a variety of edge devices and measure metrics such as accuracy, latency, and energy consumption. Controls include a baseline VGGT model and a baseline post-training quantized VGGT model.
CONTROLS: Baseline VGGT, baseline pre-quantized VGGT on clean data
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (including edge device evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect that hardware-aware quantization techniques will significantly improve the performance of VGGT on edge devices, particularly in terms of latency and energy consumption. However, we also anticipate that the optimal quantization technique may depend on the specific characteristics of the edge device, and that further research is needed to identify the most effective techniques for different edge platforms.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Baseline Model Selection and Quantization Paradigms
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the full-precision VGGT model on a set of challenging, real-world multi-view 3D reconstruction benchmarks (e.g., DTU, Replica, T-LESS) and compare its performance with the state-of-the-art. Investigate popular post-training quantization (PTQ) paradigms (e.g., PNQ, PACT, GPTQ) using 4-bit and 8-bit integer weights and activations on a similar 3D reconstruction network (e.g., a smaller-scale transformer or a DenseNet-based model) to validate their applicability to 3D tasks and identify potential issues.
CONTROLS: Compare against traditional 3D reconstruction methods (e.g., MVS, COLMAP) and ablate specific components of VGGT (e.g., the presence of special tokens).
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The full-precision VGGT model will outperform traditional 3D reconstruction methods, while PTQ paradigms will demonstrate promising results but may struggle with special tokens and high-variance activation distributions, requiring further investigation and adapting PTQ techniques for 3D reconstruction tasks.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating Activation Distribution Characteristics
PROPOSAL: Analyze the activation distribution characteristics of the full-precision VGGT model on 3D reconstruction tasks, particularly focusing on the data-independent special tokens and their impact on quantization. Utilize techniques such as histogram analysis, quantile-quantile plots, and spectral density estimation to understand the distribution shapes and features of activations across different layers and special tokens. This will provide insight into the characteristics that PTQ paradigms need to address.
CONTROLS: Compare with activations from the same model on 2D vision tasks and traditional 3D reconstruction methods.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal distinct activation distribution characteristics for special tokens, which will be heavier-tailed and more variable than regular image tokens, indicating that standard PTQ techniques may struggle to capture their properties accurately.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Special Token Adapted Post-Training Quantization
PROPOSAL: Propose a PTQ paradigm (e.g., ST-PTQ) tailored to the 3D reconstruction setting and the characteristics of special tokens. The method will incorporate specialized techniques, such as learnable quantization parameters, adaptive activation clipping, and token-specific weight initialization, to address the heavy-tailed distributions and high variance of special tokens. Experiment with ST-PTQ on a smaller-scale 3D reconstruction network to evaluate its effectiveness and identify optimal hyperparameters.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard PTQ paradigms and baseline models, and ablate individual components of ST-PTQ to assess their contributions.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ST-PTQ will demonstrate improved stability and accuracy compared to standard PTQ paradigms on 3D reconstruction tasks, but may still require further refinement to achieve optimal performance, especially when addressing high-variance activations.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Special Token Adapted Post-Training Quantization
PROPOSAL: Modify ST-PTQ to incorporate a data-driven special token pre-calibration step, which will generate representative calibration samples from a small subset of the training dataset based on the distribution of special tokens. This pre-calibration step will be used to refine the initial quantization ranges and weights, improving the robustness and generalizability of ST-PTQ on unseen scenes. Experiment with the revised ST-PTQ (ST-PTQ+) on a challenging 3D reconstruction benchmark (e.g., DTU) to evaluate its effectiveness in maintaining camera pose and geometry accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original ST-PTQ and baseline models, and ablate the pre-calibration step to assess its contributions.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ST-PTQ+ will show improved performance and robustness on 3D reconstruction tasks, particularly in scenarios with limited calibration data and diverse special token distributions, but may still require careful calibration and hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ST-PTQ+ will show improved performance and robustness on 3D reconstruction tasks, particularly in scenarios with limited calibration data and diverse special token distributions, but may still require careful calibration and hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Calibration Set Selection Strategies
PROPOSAL: Evaluate and compare different calibration set selection strategies for ST-PTQ+, including random sampling, stratified sampling, and active learning-based methods. Assess their impact on the quality of the calibration set and the overall performance of ST-PTQ+ on 3D reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of ST-PTQ+ on different calibration sets, and evaluate the robustness of the selected strategies to changes in the calibration set size and composition.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal insights into the most effective calibration set selection strategies for ST-PTQ+, which may involve combining multiple methods or adapting existing techniques to the 3D reconstruction domain.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Quantization-Aware Training for 3D Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of quantization-aware training (QAT) to 3D reconstruction transformers like VGGT, aiming to improve the robustness of the model to quantization artifacts and potentially reduce the need for extensive calibration. Use techniques such as simulated quantization noise and relaxation techniques to facilitate QAT, and evaluate the performance of QAT-trained models on 3D reconstruction benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of QAT-trained models with ST-PTQ+ and baseline models, and analyze the effect of QAT on the special tokens and activation distributions.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: QAT may lead to improved robustness and accuracy of 3D reconstruction models when quantized, but the optimal QAT regime might require careful tuning and may not generalize well to all 3D reconstruction tasks.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Automatic Mixed Precision for 3D Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of automatic mixed precision (AMP) techniques to 3D reconstruction transformers, which aim to dynamically switch between different precision levels (e.g., FP16, FP32, INT8) for different model weights and activations, depending on their computational importance and sensitivity to quantization. Evaluate the performance and energy efficiency of AMP on 3D reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance and energy efficiency of AMP with ST-PTQ+ and QAT, and analyze the effect of AMP on the special tokens and activation distributions.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: AMP may be effective in reducing energy consumption and computational overhead for 3D reconstruction tasks, but its performance may vary depending on the specific model architecture, quantization scheme, and precision levels used.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Real-World Deployment and Hardware Optimization
PROPOSAL: Conduct thorough experiments to evaluate the performance and deployability of the best-performing quantization and mixed precision methods (ST-PTQ+, QAT, and AMP) on real-world hardware (e.g., NVIDIA A100 GPUs, NVIDIA Jetson Embedded Systems). Investigate the impact of different hardware configurations and deployment scenarios on model performance, and analyze the factors influencing deployment speed and efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with performance on simulation platforms and investigate the reasons for any discrepancies.
COST: 70 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal the benefits and challenges of transferring quantized and mixed precision models to real-world hardware, highlighting opportunities for further research and development.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Lightweight and Efficient 3D Reconstruction Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate and evaluate methods to further reduce the size and computational requirements of the quantized and mixed precision 3D reconstruction models. This includes pruning, knowledge distillation, and other model compression techniques to create more efficient and lightweight models suitable for edge computing and other applications with strict resource constraints.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the compressed models with the baseline and quantized models, and analyze the trade-offs between model size, performance, and inference time.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal the feasibility of creating lightweight and efficient 3D reconstruction models that can run on resource-constrained hardware, while maintaining acceptable performance, and will highlight the need for further research in this area.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Simplifying Decision Pretrained Transformer for Continuous Control
PROPOSAL: Replacing the multi-modal output distribution in vanilla DPT with a uni-modal distribution, specifically a Gaussian distribution with learnable mean and variance, to simplify the model and force it to capture a mean-field approximation of the action posterior. This might allow for faster convergence and better generalization to unseen tasks in the multi-domain setting.
CONTROLS: Compare with vanilla DPT and assess the effect on in-context reinforcement learning performance in environments from the robot manipulation domain.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Simplified DPT should show improved stability and faster convergence, especially in the early stages of adaptation, but potentially lose some of the expressivity of the original DPT. It could fail to generalize well to very challenging or task-specific environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task DPT for Robust Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Modify DPT to jointly learn from multiple, related tasks in the pretraining phase, using a multi-task learning objective that encourages the model to share knowledge across tasks and adapt to new tasks more efficiently. This might be particularly effective in the robot manipulation and robot locomotion domains, where adjacent tasks often have a strong similarity in terms of state and action spaces.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of multi-task DPT alongside vanilla DPT and the simplified DPT (from proposal 1) in the presence of new, unseen tasks in the same domains, both with and without task-specific prompts at inference time.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Multi-task DPT should show improved performance in adapting to new tasks with related expertise, especially when transferred from a set of related tasks, but may underperform in truly novel tasks where generalization is more required. It may require a substantial dataset with sufficient task overlap to learn effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Normalizing Flows for Multi-Modal Action Distributions
PROPOSAL: Develop a normalizing flow architecture, specifically a HaarDownsample flow, to model and sample from complex multi-modal action distributions in DPT. This allows for efficient and differentiable sampling of action distributions, but would also add computational complexity in the pretraining phase.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of DPT with the HaarDownsample flow to vanilla DPT with a uni-modal Gaussian distribution (from proposal 1) and multi-task DPT (from proposal 2) in continuous-control tasks from the humanoid control and building energy management domains.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The HaarDownsample flow should enable DPT to capture highly multimodal action distributions more accurately, potentially leading to improved performance, especially in tasks with long-term dependencies. However, the added complexity may lead to divergence or exploded gradients in challenging scenarios, requiring adjustments in the training procedure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: In-Context Temporal Abstraction with DPT
PROPOSAL: Modify the inference procedure of DPT to leverage an in-context temporal abstraction mechanism that generalizes state-action pairs in the short-term past to unseen preceding states. This could be achieved by introducing a learnable fusion of recurrent neural network (RNN) and convolutional neural network (CNN) features into DPT's query embedding space. This design should be particularly useful in tasks that exhibit temporal dependencies, such as PDE control and HVAC control.
CONTROLS: Assess the contribution of this mechanism to the performance of multi-task DPT (from proposal 2) in the humanoid control and robot locomotion domains, focusing on tasks with explicit temporal relationships.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The in-context temporal abstraction mechanism should significantly enhance the ability of DPT to transfer knowledge across tasks with similar structures and dynamics. However, its effectiveness may be limited in tasks with short horizon and variable reward signals, where prior knowledge might dominate.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: In-Context Temporal Abstraction with DPT
PROPOSAL: REVISED IN-CONTEXT TEMPORAL ABSTRACTION WITH DPT: replace the RNN-based architecture in the previous proposal with a transformer-based architecture for learnable temporal feature fusion. This allows for efficient parallelization and potentially deeper exploration of temporal abstractions. Additionally, design a mechanism to incorporate a temporal prior derived from a probabilistic graphical model, to further encourage effective device usage for past experiences.
CONTROLS: Compare revised in-context temporal abstraction with the previous CNN-based approach, and investigate the effect of using a probabilistic graphical model for temporal prior in DPT-based reinforcement learning in robot locomotion and robot manipulation tasks.
COST: No change
PREDICTION: The revised architecture should exhibit enhanced performance and efficiency in tasks with temporal dependencies and also reduce sample complexity in inference time. However, the complexity of temporal abstraction with probabilistic graphical models might be challenging and more research might be needed.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Scalable Normalizing Flows for Multi-Modal Action Distributions
PROPOSAL: REVISED NORMALIZING FLOWS FOR MULTI-MODAL ACTION DISTRIBUTIONS: Consider a more efficient architecture for the normalizing flow, specifically, the FFJORD flow which utilizes a Gaussian process prior and combines the advantages of flow-based models with the efficiency of neural normals. Assess the effect of this revised architecture on the model's ability to capture complex, multi-modal distributions in various control tasks from the autonomous driving and industrial process control domains.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised normalizing flow with the original HaarDownsample flow and vanilla DPT with a uni-modal Gaussian distribution in these domains.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised normalizing flow should demonstrate improved performance and sample efficiency in capturing complex, multi-modal action distributions, potentially leading to enhanced overall learning and generalization capabilities in autonomous driving and industrial process control tasks. However, the effect on prior knowledge and feature extraction in these tasks is uncertain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Exploration via Uncertainty-Guided Sampling
PROPOSAL: Introduce an uncertainty-aware sampling mechanism that allows DPT to select the most informative next actions during exploration. This could be achieved by using the predictive variance of the model as a sampling probability, encouraging exploration in regions of high uncertainty and guiding the search towards potentially valuable areas of the state space. Assess this mechanism's contribution to the overall performance of multi-task DPT (from proposal 2) in tasks from the humanoid control and HVAC control domains, focusing on efficient exploration and task completion.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of uncertainty-guided sampling alongside a baseline of random action sampling, and compare the exploration efficiency of the two approaches in these domains.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The uncertainty-guided sampling mechanism should significantly enhance exploration efficiency, leading to faster task completion and potentially better adaptation to unseen tasks and task-specific information. However, it may require fine-tuning the exploration-exploitation trade-off, and its effectiveness may be task-dependent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Low-Dimensional Embeddings for DPT to Enhance Generalizability
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of low-dimensional embeddings, potentially learned through a contrastive learning framework, to map high-dimensional action or state spaces to a lower-dimensional, more compact representation suitable for DPT's posterior sampling mechanism. This could help to improve the model's ability to generalize across tasks and domains by reducing the dimensionality of the representation and utilizing learned structural information.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of using low-dimensional embeddings on the generalization performance of multi-task DPT (from proposal 2) in tasks from the robot manipulation and autonomous driving domains, focusing on improved out-of-distribution generalization and adaptation to unseen tasks.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The use of low-dimensional embeddings should enhance DPT's generalization capabilities, enabling it to adapt more effectively to unseen tasks and tasks in novel domains. However, the choice of embedding space and the impact of dimensionality reduction on the model's performance are uncertain and may require careful evaluation and fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning of DPT Policies for Rapid Task Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Implement a meta-learning approach to adapt DPT policies to new tasks with only a few examples, leveraging a small set of task-agnostic meta-training tasks to learn a general policy that can quickly adapt to novel tasks with minimal data. This could be achieved by using a task-agnostic loss function and a task-invariant regularization, such as a task-agnostic formulation of KL divergence.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of meta-learned DPT policies with fine-tuned DPT models and perform task-agnostic evaluation using a set of novel, unseen tasks from the humanoid control and humanoid control domains.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The meta-learned DPT policies should exhibit rapid task adaptation and improved generalizability to novel tasks, but may struggle with deeply task-specific or multimodal tasks where fine-tuning is beneficial. The effectiveness of this approach may also depend on the quality of the meta-training set and the task-agnostic loss function used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hardware-Aware Inference and Training for Large-Scale DPT Deployment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of specific hardware accelerators (e.g., GPUs with large memory, TPUs, or specialized ICs) to speed up DPT inference and training, potentially leading to significant cost savings and real-world deployability. This could be achieved by designing model pruning, knowledge distillation, and memory-efficient inference techniques tailored to the hardware accelerators' strengths and limitations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of hardware-aware optimization techniques on computational resources, accuracy, and deployment time, using evaluation environments from the robot manipulation and HVAC control domains.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (coalesced with the deployment process)
PREDICTION: Successful hardware-aware optimization should make DPT more deployable and scalable, but the effectiveness would depend on factors like the specific hardware and the real-world deployment context.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Multi-Modal Action Representation for Scalable DPT
PROPOSAL:  We propose a multi-modal action representation for DPT, which combines a discrete action set with a continuous latent action space. This allows the model to capture complex and multi-modal action distributions in continuous-control environments. Specifically, we introduce a novel action embedding layer that outputs a joint representation of discrete and continuous actions, which is then used to condition the action distribution over continuous actions.
CONTROLS:  We compare our approach to vanilla DPT and also include ablated versions with only discrete or only continuous action spaces.
COST:  100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This approach should improve the scalability of DPT to continuous-control environments, and we expect to see improved performance on the robot manipulation and robot locomotion tasks, but encounter challenges on tasks with highly variable and context-dependent action distributions, such as HVAC control.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Efficient Sampling of Continuous Actions for DPT
PROPOSAL:  To efficiently sample from the multi-modal action distribution learned by our proposed action representation, we introduce a variant of the Gumbel-softmax estimator that takes into account the discrete action set. This allows the model to efficiently sample actions that conform to the discrete action set, while still leveraging the expressiveness of the continuous latent space. We also propose a temperature schedule that adjusts the sampling process as the agent adapts to new environments.
CONTROLS:  We compare our approach to naive uniform sampling and entropy-regularized sampling on the continuous action space.
COST:  200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This approach should improve the sample efficiency and overall performance of our DPT variant on tasks that require frequent sampling from complex action distributions, such as humanoid control and building energy management, but may struggle with extremely high-dimensional action spaces like autonomous driving.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Task-Adaptive Temperature Scaling for DPT
PROPOSAL:  We propose a task-adaptive temperature scaling technique that adjusts the temperature parameter of the Gumbel-softmax estimator based on the task-specific complexity. By encoding the task-specific complexity into a scalar value, we can adapt the temperature parameter to optimize the sampling process for each individual task. This allows our DPT variant to adapt to new and unseen tasks without require retraining, and leverage the expressiveness of the continuous action space while maintaining the benefits of the discrete action set.
CONTROLS:  We compare our approach to a fixed temperature schedule and a temperature schedule learned through meta-learning.
COST:  150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This approach should improve the task-adaptability and overall performance of our DPT variant, and we expect to see consistent improvements across a range of tasks, with potential for significant improvements on tasks that exhibit significant task-specific complexity, such as indoor robotic manipulation and HVAC control.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Memory-Augmented DPT for Long-Horizon Tasks
PROPOSAL:  We propose a memory-augmented variant of DPT that stores a fixed-length context vector summarizing the agent's recent experiences. This allows the model to leverage past experiences to inform its current decision-making process, enabling it to handle long-horizon tasks that require coordination across multiple time steps. The context vector is updated incrementally as new experiences are acquired, allowing the model to dynamically adapt to changing environments.
CONTROLS:  We compare our approach to vanilla DPT and a baseline with an external memory component.
COST:  300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This approach should improve the ability of our DPT variant to handle long-horizon tasks and plan across multiple time steps, with potential applications in tasks such as robot locomotion and PDE control. However, we may encounter challenges in terms of memory size and complexity, particularly for tasks that require high-capacity memory representations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Revising Memory-Augmented DPT for Effective Context Utilization
PROPOSAL:  We revise the memory-augmented DPT component to use a more efficient memory architecture that allows for effective context utilization. Specifically, we introduce a hierarchical memory structure that consists of a short-term memory and a long-term memory. The short-term memory is used to store recent experiences, while the long-term memory is used to store distilled knowledge from previous tasks. This architecture allows our DPT variant to leverage past experiences more effectively and adapt to new tasks more quickly.
CONTROLS:  We compare our revised architecture to the original memory-augmented DPT and a baseline with an external memory component.
COST:  220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This revision should improve the performance and adaptability of our DPT variant, particularly in tasks that require coordination across multiple time steps, such as humanoid control and building energy management.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Revising 4. Memory-Augmented DPT for Long-Horizon Tasks
PROPOSAL:  We revise the memory-augmented DPT component to improve the interaction between the memory and the decision-making process. Specifically, we introduce a memory-aware residual connection that allows the memory vector to influence the decision-making process. This architecture enables our DPT variant to leverage past experiences more effectively and adapt to new tasks more quickly.
CONTROLS:  We compare our revised architecture to the original memory-augmented DPT and a baseline with an external memory component.
COST:  220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This revision should improve the performance and adaptability of our DPT variant, particularly in tasks that require coordination across multiple time steps, such as humanoid control and building energy management.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Multi-Agent Extensions for DPT in Multi-Robot Systems
PROPOSAL:  We propose a multi-agent extension of DPT that allow our agent to interact with other robots in a multi-robot system. Specifically, we introduce a centralized learning architecture that allows the agent to learn from the experiences of other robots in the system, while also coordinating its own actions with respect to the other robots. We also propose a distributed learning architecture that allows multiple robots to learn and cooperate with each other in real-time.
CONTROLS:  We compare our multi-agent extensions to a baseline single-agent architecture and a fully decentralized approach.
COST:  350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This extension should improve the performance and cooperation of our DPT variant in multi-robot systems, with potential applications in tasks such as robot locomotion and industrial process control.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Transfer Learning from Synthetic to Real-World DPT
PROPOSAL:  We explore transfer learning techniques that allow our DPT variant to leverage knowledge learned from synthetic, simulated environments and adapt it to real-world domains. Specifically, we investigate using domain adaptation techniques, such as adversarial training and feature alignment, to transfer the knowledge learned from synthetic environments to real-world tasks. We also propose a framework for meta-learning that allows our agent to learn how to adapt to new tasks and domains.
CONTROLS:  We compare our transfer learning approaches to a baseline approach that uses only real-world data and a cross-validation approach that uses domain-specific data.
COST:  280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  This approach should improve the performance and adaptability of our DPT variant in real-world environments, such as autonomous driving and industrial process control, by leveraging knowledge learned from synthetic environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Uncertainty-Aware DPT for Real-World Environments
PROPOSAL:  We propose an uncertainty-aware extension of DPT that allows our agent to incorporate uncertainty estimates into its decision-making process. PROPOSAL 1: Multi-Modal Action Representation for Scalable DPT
We propose a multi-modal action representation for DPT, which combines a discrete action set with a continuous latent action space. This allows the model to capture complex and multi-modal action distributions in continuous-control environments. Specifically, we introduce a novel action embedding layer that outputs a joint representation of discrete and continuous actions, which is then used to condition the action distribution over continuous actions.
Controls: We compare our approach to vanilla DPT and also include ablated versions with only discrete or only continuous action spaces.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should improve the scalability of DPT to continuous-control environments, and we expect to see improved performance on the robot manipulation and robot locomotion tasks, but encounter challenges on tasks with highly variable and context-dependent action distributions, such as HVAC control.

PROPOSAL 2: Efficient Sampling of Continuous Actions for DPT
To efficiently sample from the multi-modal action distribution learned by our proposed action representation, we introduce a variant of the Gumbel-softmax estimator that takes into account the discrete action set. This allows the model to efficiently sample actions that conform to the discrete action set, while still leveraging the expressiveness of the continuous latent space. We also propose a temperature schedule that adjusts the sampling process as the agent adapts to new environments.
Controls: We compare our approach to naive uniform sampling and entropy-regularized sampling on the continuous action space.
Estimated cost: 200 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should improve the sample efficiency and overall performance of our DPT variant on tasks that require frequent sampling from complex action distributions, such as humanoid control and building energy management, but may struggle with extremely high-dimensional action spaces like autonomous driving.

PROPOSAL 3: Task-Adaptive Temperature Scaling for DPT
We propose a task-adaptive temperature scaling technique that adjusts the temperature parameter of the Gumbel-softmax estimator based on the task-specific complexity. By encoding the task-specific complexity into a scalar value, we can adapt the temperature parameter to optimize the sampling process for each individual task. This allows our DPT variant to adapt to new and unseen tasks without require retraining, and leverage the expressiveness of the continuous action space while maintaining the benefits of the discrete action set.
Controls: We compare our approach to a fixed temperature schedule and a temperature schedule learned through meta-learning.
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should improve the task-adaptability and overall performance of our DPT variant, and we expect to see consistent improvements across a range of tasks, with potential for significant improvements on tasks that exhibit significant task-specific complexity, such as indoor robotic manipulation and HVAC control.

PROPOSAL 4: Memory-Augmented DPT for Long-Horizon Tasks
We propose a memory-augmented variant of DPT that stores a fixed-length context vector summarizing the agent's recent experiences. This allows the model to leverage past experiences to inform its current decision-making process, enabling it to handle long-horizon tasks that require coordination across multiple time steps. The context vector is updated incrementally as new experiences are acquired, allowing the model to dynamically adapt to changing environments.
Controls: We compare our approach to vanilla DPT and a baseline with an external memory component.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should improve the ability of our DPT variant to handle long-horizon tasks and plan across multiple time steps, with potential applications in tasks such as robot locomotion and PDE control. However, we may encounter challenges in terms of memory size and complexity, particularly for tasks that require high-capacity memory representations.

PROPOSAL 5: Multi-Agent Extensions for DPT in Multi-Robot Systems
We propose a multi-agent extension of DPT that allow our agent to interact with other robots in a multi-robot system. Specifically, we introduce a centralized learning architecture that allows the agent to learn from the experiences of other robots in the system, while also coordinating its own actions with respect to the other robots. We also propose a distributed learning architecture that allows multiple robots to learn and cooperate with each other in real-time.
Controls: We compare our multi-agent extensions to a baseline single-agent architecture and a fully decentralized approach.
Estimated cost: 350 GPU-hours
Prediction: This extension should improve the performance and cooperation of our DPT variant in multi-robot systems, with potential applications in tasks such as robot locomotion and industrial process control.

We explore transfer learning techniques that allow our DPT variant to leverage knowledge learned from synthetic, simulated environments and adapt it to real-world domains. Specifically, we investigate using domain adaptation techniques, such as adversarial training and feature alignment, to transfer the knowledge learned from synthetic environments to real-world tasks. We also propose a framework for meta-learning that allows our agent to learn how to adapt to new tasks and domains.

TITLE: Investigating the Expressiveness of Transformer-based Action Distributions for Continuous Control Tasks
PROPOSAL: Experimentally evaluate vanilla DPT and its variants on a synthetic simulator of a diverse set of continuous-control tasks, specifically focusing on its action distribution modeling. Utilize a mixture of Gaussian distributions or a normalizing flow to capture complex action distributions.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline variant of DPT with a fixed, pre-defined action prior (e.g., a simple diagonal Gaussian), and ablate the different action distribution architectures to evaluate their impact on in-context learning performance.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Vanilla DPT will underperform compared to variants exploiting more expressive action priors, and models with normalizing flows will show better adaptability than mixture models. The challenge lies in reasonably generalizing to unseen tasks, with potentially poor performance on tasks requiring extreme action vectors.

TITLE: Scaling DPT with Neural Gaussian Processes for Multi-Modal Continuous Control Tasks
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural variant of the Gaussian Process (GP) that incorporates the Transformer-based architecture of DPT for modeling uncertain action distributions. This will enable the agent to learn to approximate complex multi-modal action posteriors and explore the search space more effectively.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against vanilla DPT, a GP-based version without the neural augmentation, and a mixture of experts (MoE) variant that combines multiple DPT models with different prior distributions.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The neural GP variant will show significant improvement in handling complex, multi-modal continuous action spaces and achieving better in-context learning performance, although it might also increase the risk of overfitting to some extent.

PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Instead of fully implementing neural GP, focus on incorporating a GP-based prior into DPT's Transformer architecture. CONTROLS: Keep the comparison with vanilla DPT, and also evaluate the robustness of the GP-based prior against tasks with varying levels of noise and task-structure variability.

PREDICTION: The GP-based prior will mitigate overfitting and improve exploration-exploitation trade-offs, especially on more uncertain or partially-observed tasks, but introduce significant computational overhead and may not generalize as well to significantly different control tasks due to the conditioning process.
